lead: Pentecost opens the Season of the Apostles, and its four readings show how God makes a people his own. At Sinai, in the third month after the Exodus, God offers Israel a covenant: they will be his treasured possession, a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. In Jerusalem, on the feast that remembered the harvest and, for many Jews, the gift of the Law, the Spirit comes with wind and fire, and the apostles speak so that every nation hears in its own language. Paul tells the Corinthians that the one Spirit gives many gifts for the common good. In John, Jesus promises that the Spirit of truth will guide his disciples into all the truth. The words to watch are covenant, fire and truth. What began at Sinai with one people is opened to all.

r.h: A priestly kingdom and a holy nation
set: Israel has crossed the sea, been fed with manna and given water from the rock. Now, in the third month, they reach the mountain where God first spoke to Moses from the bush (3:12). Here the covenant will be made and the Law given (chapters 19–24).

Later Jewish tradition came to celebrate the giving of the Law at Sinai on the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival kept fifty days after Passover. That is why this reading stands beside Acts 2 today: the Church’s Pentecost is the new Sinai, where the law is written not on stone but on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
str: vv. 1–2: arrival at Sinai, in the third month; Israel camps before the mountain.
vv. 3–4: God calls Moses: “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.”
vv. 5–6: the offer: if you keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession, a priestly kingdom, a holy nation.
vv. 7–8: Moses sets the words before the elders; the people answer as one.
v. 9: God will come in a dense cloud, so that the people may hear and believe.
kw: A king’s private treasure, the jewels he keeps for himself. The whole earth is God’s, but Israel is his own jewel, chosen not to be proud but to serve.
A people set between God and the nations, as priests stand between God and the people. Israel’s calling is for the sake of the world.
Holy means set apart for God. Israel is to be different from the nations so as to show them who God is.
vv: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.

The covenant begins with grace, not with a command. God first reminds Israel of what he has done; only then does he ask for their answer. The goal of the Exodus is not a place but a person: “to myself”.
you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples. Indeed, the whole earth is mine
Election is not favouritism. The God of the whole earth chooses one people so that through them he may bless all (Genesis 12:3).
but you shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.

St Peter applies these words to the baptized: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people” (1 Peter 2:9). The Church does not take Israel’s place; she is brought into Israel’s calling.
The people all answered as one: “Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do.”
A single voice, a single answer. At Pentecost the many languages will again make one confession of faith.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the chosen people was constituted by God as “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation”, and that the whole Church, the new people of God, shares in Christ’s priesthood (CCC 1539, 1546). The Second Vatican Council quotes 1 Peter 2:9 when it teaches the common priesthood of the faithful, by which the baptized offer spiritual sacrifices and share in offering the Eucharist (Lumen Gentium 10). Many Fathers saw in Sinai, with its fire, cloud and voice, a figure of Pentecost: there the Law was given on tablets of stone; here the Spirit writes it in hearts (in substance, St Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter 17).

set: The disciples have been waiting in Jerusalem, as the Risen Lord told them, for the promise of the Father (1:4–5). The Twelve are complete again (1:26). Now comes the Feast of Weeks, called in Greek Pentecost, one of the three pilgrim feasts when Jews came from far and wide to the Temple. That is why the city is full of “devout Jews from every nation under heaven”.

Luke tells the event with signs from Israel’s Scriptures. Wind and fire recall Sinai, where the Lord descended in fire and the whole mountain shook (Exodus 19:18). The many languages recall Babel, where human pride ended in confusion and scattering (Genesis 11:1–9).
str: v. 1: the day of Pentecost; all together in one place.
vv. 2–3: a sound like wind; tongues as of fire resting on each.
v. 4: filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages.
vv. 5–11: the crowd from every nation hears God’s deeds of power in its own language.
vv. 12–13: amazement and mockery: “What does this mean?” “They are filled with new wine.”
kw: Literally “was being fulfilled”. Luke uses the word for the coming of a promised time (as in Luke 9:51). The feast itself reaches its fulfilment.
Luke uses pnoē, a blast of wind, beside pneuma, Spirit. In Hebrew one word, rûaḥ, means both wind and spirit, as in the breath that moved over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2).
The word of verses 6 and 8, the language one learned at home. The Gospel does not erase the languages and cultures of the nations; it speaks in each of them.
vv: When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.
“All together”: the one hundred twenty, with the apostles and Mary (1:14–15). The Spirit comes to a community at prayer.
Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.
One fire, divided so that each receives it. The Spirit is given to the Church and to each member personally.
Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia
The list begins in the east, beyond the Roman Empire, in the lands where the Church of the East would grow. Our own Church’s tradition traces its family to these very regions.
in our own languages we hear them speaking about God’s deeds of power.
The content of their speech is praise: the mighty works of God. Babel tried to make a name for itself (Genesis 11:4); Pentecost proclaims the name of God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ’s Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and that on that day the Holy Trinity is fully revealed (CCC 731–732). The Church, it says, was made manifest to the world on the day of Pentecost by the outpouring of the Spirit (CCC 1076). St Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on Pentecost, contrasts the confusion of tongues at Babel, which scattered the proud, with the gift of tongues at Pentecost, which gathers all into one (in substance, Oration 41).

set: The Corinthians were rich in spiritual gifts and proud of them. Some prized speaking in tongues above all and looked down on those without it (see chapters 12–14). Paul does not reject the gifts; he puts them in order. They come from one Spirit, they serve the one body, and the greatest of all, as chapter 13 will show, is love.
str: vv. 1–3: the test of the Spirit: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
vv. 4–6: varieties of gifts, services and activities; the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God.
v. 7: each gift is a manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
vv. 8–10: a list of nine gifts.
v. 11: one Spirit gives to each as he chooses.
kw: Gifts of grace, from charis, grace. A charism is not a reward for holiness but a gift for service.
Perhaps the oldest Christian creed, spoken at baptism (Romans 10:9). In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios stands for the divine name. To call Jesus Lord is to confess him as God.
What benefits all together. A gift kept for oneself has missed its purpose.
vv: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
Faith itself is the first gift of the Spirit. Every Christian who confesses Christ already shows that the Spirit is at work.
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God
Spirit, Lord, God: Paul’s pattern is already Trinitarian. The unity of the Church reflects the unity of the one God in three persons.
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
“To each”: no one in the Church is without a gift, and no gift is for private glory.
All these are activated by one and the same Spirit, who allots to each one individually just as the Spirit chooses.
The Spirit chooses, as the Lord chose Matthias. We do not choose our gifts; we receive them and put them to use.
ch: The Catechism teaches that charisms, whether extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit which directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered to her building up, to the good of all and to the needs of the world (CCC 799). Charity is the true measure of them (CCC 800), and discernment of charisms belongs to those who lead the Church, who must not extinguish the Spirit but test everything (CCC 801; Lumen Gentium 12).

r.h: He will guide you into all the truth
set: These words are spoken at the Last Supper, on the night before Jesus died (John 13–17). Jesus is preparing his friends for his departure. They are full of sorrow. He tells them that his going is for their good, because only then will the Advocate come. Here come the last two of the five sayings about the Spirit in the Supper discourse (14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26; 16:7–11; 16:13–15).
str: vv. 5–7: sorrow at his going; it is to your advantage, for the Advocate will come.
vv. 8–11: the Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment.
vv. 12–13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.
vv. 14–15: he will glorify me; all that the Father has is mine.
kw: One called to stand beside another: a defender in court, a helper, a comforter. Jesus has been their Advocate; he will send “another” (14:16).
A word from the law court: to expose, to bring to the light. The Spirit reverses the world’s verdict on Jesus. The one it condemned is shown to be righteous.
To lead along a road, as a guide leads travellers. The Spirit does not give a new Gospel; he leads the disciples deeper into the truth that is Christ (14:6).
vv: Nevertheless I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you
The disciples wanted Jesus to stay as he was. He gives them something greater: his presence within them through the Spirit.
about sin, because they do not believe in me; about righteousness, because I am going to the Father
The deepest sin is unbelief, refusing the light. Jesus’ going to the Father, through the Cross and Resurrection, is the Father’s verdict that he is righteous.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but will speak whatever he hears
The Spirit speaks what he hears, as the Son speaks what he hears from the Father (8:26). The Trinity is a communion of listening and giving.
All that the Father has is mine. For this reason I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.
The Spirit’s work is to make Christ known. Wherever the Spirit is truly at work, Christ is glorified.
ch: The Catechism gathers these promises: the Spirit of truth, the other Paraclete, will teach the disciples everything, remind them of all that Christ said, bear witness to him, lead them into all truth, glorify Christ, and prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (CCC 729). Pope St John Paul II devoted a large part of his encyclical on the Holy Spirit, Dominum et Vivificantem (1986), to the words “he will convince the world concerning sin”. The Second Vatican Council teaches that through the Spirit the understanding of the apostolic Tradition grows in the Church, as she advances towards the fullness of divine truth (Dei Verbum 8).

qa: Did the apostles speak foreign languages, or did the crowd hear a miracle?

Luke stresses both: they “began to speak in other languages” (2:4), and each one “heard them speaking in the native language of each” (2:6). Whether the wonder was in the speaking or in the hearing, the sign is the same: the Gospel is for every people, in its own tongue. This is different from the gift of tongues at Corinth, which needed an interpreter (1 Corinthians 14:27).
Does the Spirit bring new revelations beyond Christ?

No. Jesus says the Spirit “will take what is mine and declare it to you” (16:14). The Church teaches that the Christian economy will never pass away and that no new public revelation is to be expected before the glorious coming of Christ (Dei Verbum 4; CCC 66). The Spirit leads the Church deeper into what Christ has revealed, so that its meaning is grasped more fully over the centuries.
Why is Pentecost linked to Sinai?

In Exodus, Israel reaches Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, about the time of the harvest festival. Later Jewish tradition remembered the giving of the Law on the Feast of Weeks. Luke tells the coming of the Spirit with signs of Sinai: a sound from heaven, fire, a people gathered. For Christians, the Spirit fulfils what Jeremiah promised, a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34).
rite: With Pentecost the Syro-Malabar Church begins the Season of the Apostles (Shleeha), which remembers the Church’s first mission under the Spirit. It suits our Church that the list of nations at Pentecost begins with “Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia”: the Church of the East grew in those lands, and from that Church our ancestors in Malabar received their liturgy and their bishops for many centuries, while they kept the faith first preached, by our tradition, by Mar Thoma Shleeha, who was in the upper room (Acts 1:13).

At every Holy Qurbana, in the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, the priest asks that the Holy Spirit come and rest upon the offering, bless it and sanctify it, for the pardon of sins and the hope of resurrection. Pentecost is not only a memory; it happens again on our altars and in us. This is a good day to renew our confirmation, the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit, and to ask what gift the Spirit has given each of us for the common good.
study: God reminded Israel, “I bore you on eagles’ wings,” before asking for obedience. What has God done for me that I need to remember before I answer him?
At Pentecost each one heard the Gospel in his own language. How can my family and parish speak the faith in the language of young people, the poor and those far away?
Paul says each one is given a gift for the common good. What gift has the Spirit given me, and how am I using it?
Jesus said his going away was for his disciples’ good. Where in my life has a loss opened the way for the Spirit?
